recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Long strands of dark dust stand out against the yellowish core of NGC 4150, an elliptical galaxy 44 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. Elliptical galaxies were long thought to have finished making stars billions of years ago, but this one still holds young ones.

Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 found clumps of young, blue stars, significantly less than a billion years old, tracing a ring around the center that rotates with the galaxy. That stellar nursery is about 1,300 light-years across. From the stars' colors, the team worked out that the burst of star birth began about a billion years ago and has since slowed, while most of the galaxy's stars are around 10 billion years old.

The astronomers believe the fuel arrived with a small, gas-rich galaxy that merged with NGC 4150 around one billion years ago. The young stars contain very few heavy elements, which points to a metal-poor dwarf galaxy about one-twentieth the mass of NGC 4150.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, built from several filter images. F814W is shown in red, F555W in green and F438W in blue.
understand.eye: The exposures add up to 3.8 hours, gathering far more light than the eye can, and the colors come from separate filter images.

explore: Minor mergers like this are thought to happen up to 10 times more often than clashes between large galaxies, but they leave little trace. Ultraviolet light helps, because it picks out the faint blue glow of hot young stars against the old red stars that dominate ellipticals. Team member Joseph Silk says young stars give at least a third of all elliptical galaxies a blue glow.
sources: NASA release: Hubble Captures New Life in an Ancient Galaxy
